519.title: Looking back: no excuse
519.hook: a discourse we passed: Sariputta tells a brahmin that duty to family does not excuse harming others
519.howItsDone: Buddhist ethics across schools honors support for parents and family as a duty while holding that right livelihood, earning without harming others, is part of the eightfold path; MN 97 is one place this is spelled out.

segments.voice: Yesterday, looking back: Ghatikara the potter, who cared for his blind parents and kept the precepts. Your line: the good potter. Today, another discourse we walked past, and a man who wasn't so honest.

I'm doing it for my family. People say it about the best things they do, and sometimes about the worst. In the ninety-seventh discourse, Sariputta hears news of an old acquaintance, a brahmin named Dhananjani who works for the king. He's gotten careless, people say. He uses the king's authority to squeeze the brahmin householders, and uses the householders as cover to cheat the king. Sariputta goes to find him.
screen: `I'M DOING IT FOR MY FAMILY.` → `DHANANJANI, THE KING'S MAN.` → `SARIPUTTA GOES TO FIND HIM.`

segments.voice: He finds him at a cowshed while the cows are being milked. Dhananjani offers fresh milk; Sariputta has already eaten for the day, and asks: Dhananjani, are you diligent? How can I be? the brahmin answers. I have my parents to support. A wife and children. Workers. Duties to friends, to ancestors, to the gods, to the king. And this body has to be fed too. It's an honest list, and a heavy one. Sariputta doesn't dismiss it. He asks a question. Suppose a man broke the moral law for his parents' sake, and when he died, the wardens of the hell realms dragged him off. Could he say: I did it for my parents, let me go? Could his parents say: he did it for us, let him go? No, says Dhananjani. Then the same question for wife and children, workers, friends, ancestors, the gods, the king, this body. No, every time. One more. Who's better: the one who does wrong for his parents, or the one who does right for them? The one who does right. Then there are other ways, Sariputta says, in line with the dhamma, to earn a living, support your parents, and do no harm. The Pali word is dhammika: righteous, in keeping with the dhamma. Family duty isn't the problem; elsewhere the discourses honor it. But love for your own doesn't turn harm to others into something else. The duty stays. The excuse goes.
screen: `AT THE COWSHED, MILK OFFERED` · `I HAVE SO MANY TO SUPPORT` · `COULD HE SAY: I DID IT FOR THEM?` · `THERE ARE RIGHTEOUS WAYS` · then, large: `NO EXCUSE.`

segments.voice: Let one excuse you use come up, I'm too busy, everyone does it, it's for the kids, and hold it gently, the way Sariputta held Dhananjani's list. Is the duty real? Probably; now ask whether there's a way to meet it without the harm, and just see one other way, without solving it all.
Looking back. A second discourse we passed: duty to family is real, but it never makes harming others right.
Your line: no excuse. There's a righteous way to carry the same load. Day five hundred nineteen, done.

520.title: Your favorite discourse
520.hook: of the Majjhima read so far, which one stays
520.howItsDone: Many Buddhists return to a few discourses again and again; in Theravada communities some are chanted as paritta for protection and blessing, and some teachers assign students one discourse to study closely for a long time.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dhananjani at the cowshed, and your line, no excuse. Duty is real; harm done for it is still harm. Today, no new discourse, just a question for you.

About four months ago we opened the Middle-Length Sayings. Since then: a raft, a saw, a snake grabbed by the tail. A hen sitting on her eggs. A murderer turned monk. A fire that goes out and goes nowhere. Seven chariots in relay. A potter's roof. Much of it may have blurred, the way books do. But maybe one picture stuck, one you've thought about in the shower, or told a friend.
screen: `A RAFT, A SAW, A SNAKE.` → `A HEN, A FIRE, SEVEN CHARIOTS.` → `WHICH ONE STAYED?`

segments.voice: Having a favorite isn't a modern habit. The word for a discourse is sutta, which some readers explain as a thread, the Pali form of the Sanskrit sutra. A thread is something you can pick up again. And Buddhist communities pick up some threads more than others. In Theravada communities, certain discourses are chanted for protection and blessing. Some teachers return again and again to a handful, like the one on mindfulness of breathing, or the verse about one fine night: don't chase the past, don't pin hopes on the future. The discourses suggest why. Remember the day we counted feelings: two, three, five, six, eighteen, thirty-six, a hundred and eight. Each count, the Buddha said, was a way of teaching fitted to the listener. Different people needed different doors. So a favorite isn't a ranking of the teaching. It's a clue to where you are. If the saw stayed with you, maybe you're working with anger. If it was the raft, maybe with holding on too tight to ideas. The hen on her eggs, maybe with patience. There's a caution too, from the water snake discourse: grab a teaching by the wrong end and it bites. So ask not only which line you like, but how you're holding it. And here's a good test of a favorite: read it whole again, setting and questions and all. Often it says more, or something slightly different, than the version you've been carrying.
screen: `SUTTA: A THREAD TO PICK UP` · `COMMUNITIES HAVE FAVORITES TOO` · `A FAVORITE SHOWS WHERE YOU ARE` · `READ IT WHOLE AGAIN` · then, large: `YOURS.`

Sutta. A thread: the discourse that stayed with you, a clue to where you are, best tested by reading it whole again.
Your line: yours. A favorite is a clue to where you stand, not a ranking. See you tomorrow.

521.title: The Middle-Length, closed
521.hook: from the root of all things to the training of the senses
521.howItsDone: The Majjhima Nikaya is one of the five collections of the Sutta Pitaka in the Pali Canon, studied and recited in Theravada monasteries; many of its discourses have parallels in the Chinese Madhyama Agama, preserved by another early school.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sutta, a thread, and your line, yours. A favorite is a clue to where you are. Today we close the whole Middle-Length collection.

The first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings ends on a strange note. The text says the monks did not delight in what the Buddha had said about the root of all things. It doesn't say why. The last discourse ends with a young brahmin sitting silent and a quiet teaching about eyes that stay open. In between, a hundred and fifty more.
screen: `THE FIRST: THE MONKS WERE NOT PLEASED.` → `THE LAST: EYES THAT STAY OPEN.` → `A HUNDRED AND FIFTY IN BETWEEN.`

segments.voice: The Pali name is Majjhima Nikaya: the middle collection. Middle here means middle-length, not as long as the long discourses, not as short as the connected ones. It's arranged in three groups of fifty, the root fifty, the middle fifty and the last fifty, and the last group has two extra, which is how you get a hundred and fifty-two. Here's the road we walked. The root of all things, and all the taints. Heirs in dhamma, not in things. Fear met in the forest at night. The stained cloth that won't take the dye. The saw, and goodwill even under it. The water snake and the raft. Relay chariots. The noble search. Milk and water. Saccaka sweating. Examine even the teacher. Rahula and the mirror, then the earth. Angulimala, read whole. Any wood makes fire. Breathing in sixteen steps. A hall empty of elephants. One fine night. Punna going west. Rahula freed under a tree, six sets of six, and finally, seeing without being swept. Now the small surprise in the name. Majjhima is the same word as the middle in the middle way, majjhima patipada, the path between indulgence and self-torment that the Buddha named in his first teaching. The title is about length, not doctrine. But the collection keeps showing that path anyway: not grabbing, not pushing away, not shutting the eyes, not drowning in what they see. A hundred and fifty-two ways of walking down the middle.

Your line: the middle way, in words. The shelf is closed; the path it kept showing is still open. That's day five hundred twenty-one.

522.title: The Long Discourses
522.hook: thirty-four long discourses, many set as stories and conversations
522.howItsDone: The Digha Nikaya is the first of the five collections of discourses in the Pali Canon; Theravada monastics study it, and some of its discourses, like the one on the foundations of mindfulness, are recited and widely taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday we closed the Middle-Length Sayings, and your line, the middle way, in words. Today a new shelf, with fewer books and longer ones.

A king on his palace roof on a full-moon night, asking his ministers which teacher to visit. A brahmin with hundreds of animals tied up for a sacrifice. A monk climbing through heaven after heaven with a question no god can answer. The Buddha's last journey, step by step, to the grove where he lay down for the last time. These are all in one collection, and it's only thirty-four discourses long.
screen: `A KING ON A MOONLIT ROOF.` → `A MONK CLIMBING THROUGH HEAVENS.` → `THE LAST JOURNEY.`

segments.voice: The Pali name is Digha Nikaya, the long collection; digha just means long. Thirty-four discourses, some as long as a short book, in three parts. The first, thirteen discourses, is named for morality, because each one contains the same long passage on a monk's conduct. The second, the great division, holds the big set pieces: the Buddha's final days, the great discourse on the foundations of mindfulness. The third gathers the rest, including the advice to a young householder named Sigala on how to treat parents, teachers, spouse, friends and workers. Where the Middle-Length Sayings often talk to monks, the long ones often talk to outsiders: kings, wealthy brahmins, wandering philosophers, a curious householder. Many are stories with a setting and a plot. Someone arrives with a question, a challenge, sometimes a grudge, and leaves changed, or not. Some scholars suggest this collection was especially suited to presenting the teaching to people who weren't yet followers. That's a theory, and others weigh it differently. In English, an early translation came from Thomas Rhys Davids, later joined by Caroline Rhys Davids, under the title Dialogues of the Buddha, starting in 1899. That name fits. Over the next weeks we'll read the first thirteen in order: praise and blame, the net of views, a king's moonlit ride, a proud young brahmin, a sacrifice with no blood, the line of the blind.
screen: `DIGHA: LONG, THIRTY-FOUR OF THEM` · `THREE PARTS: MORALITY, GREAT, THE REST` · `OFTEN SPEAKING TO OUTSIDERS` · `DIALOGUES, TAKEN A PIECE AT A TIME` · then, large: `THE LONG ONES.`

Notice which one pulls at you, even a little, without deciding why, and rest with the breath.

523.title: Praise and blame
523.hook: if others praise or blame the Buddha, the monks should be neither elated nor angry
523.howItsDone: Buddhist teachers across schools speak of the eight worldly winds (gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain), and practitioners train to meet them with equanimity, as the opening of DN 1 describes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Digha Nikaya, the long collection, and your line, the long ones. Today it begins, on a dusty road.

The first long discourse starts on the road between Rajagaha and Nalanda. The Buddha is walking with a large group of monks. Behind them, on the same road, come two more travelers: a wandering teacher named Suppiya and his young student Brahmadatta. And all the way, they argue. Suppiya is running down the Buddha, his teaching and his monks. His own student is praising all three. That night everyone stops at the same rest house.
screen: `THE ROAD TO NALANDA.` → `ONE BLAMES, ONE PRAISES.` → `THE SAME REST HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Next morning the monks are talking it over: the two of them, one praising and one blaming, all the way down the road. The Buddha walks in, asks what they're discussing, and gives the instruction that opens the whole long collection. If others speak against me, or the teaching, or the community, don't be angry or resentful or upset. That would be an obstacle for you. And if you were angry, could you even tell whether what they said was true or false? The monks admit they couldn't. So if something said is false, calmly explain that it's false: that isn't so, that isn't found among us. Then the other half, easier to miss. If others speak in praise of me, or the teaching, or the community, don't be elated or delighted or puffed up. That too would be an obstacle. If what they say is true, simply acknowledge it: yes, that's so, that's found among us. The Pali words are vanna and avanna: praise and dispraise. Notice the symmetry. Praise is treated as just as risky as blame. Both cloud the mind, and a clouded mind can't check facts. The point isn't to stop caring what's true. It's the opposite: stay level, so you can see what's true. And the monks are told to do it for their own teacher, not just for themselves. Even loyalty is supposed to stay calm.
screen: `THE MONKS TALK IT OVER` · `BLAME: DON'T BE ANGRY` · `PRAISE: DON'T BE ELATED` · `STAY LEVEL TO SEE WHAT'S TRUE` · then, large: `NOT ELATED, NOT ANGRY.`

Vanna. Praise, with its opposite avanna, dispraise: neither to be angry at nor elated by, so the mind stays clear enough to tell what's true.
Your line: not elated, not angry. A level mind is the one that can check the facts. Day five hundred twenty-three, done.

524.title: The small things
524.hook: the Buddha refrains from even small unkindness, like idle talk and shows
524.carry: the ground the summit stands on
524.howItsDone: Lay Buddhists keep five precepts, and in Theravada communities some take eight on observance days, which add refraining from entertainments, adornment and luxurious beds: a lay echo of the conduct listed in DN 1.

segments.voice: Yesterday: vanna and avanna, praise and blame on the road, and your line, not elated, not angry. Today, what people actually praise the Buddha for.

Board games on eight-row and ten-row boards. Games played on imaginary boards in the air. Dice. Toy plows and toy windmills. Guessing what a friend is thinking. Elephant fights, ballad singers, acrobats. This is a real list, from the first long discourse, a snapshot of what people did for fun long ago. It's there because the Buddha is describing what he doesn't do. These little things, he says, are what an ordinary person praises him for.
screen: `DICE, BOARD GAMES, ELEPHANT FIGHTS.` → `A SNAPSHOT OF ANCIENT FUN.` → `WHAT PEOPLE PRAISE HIM FOR.`

segments.voice: When an ordinary person praises me, he tells the monks, it's for small matters, mere moral conduct. Then he lists them. He's put down the stick and the sword. He's gentle and kind, compassionate toward all living beings. He takes only what's given. He speaks the truth; he's reliable. He doesn't carry tales from one group to another to split them apart; he brings together those who are divided, and enjoys harmony. His speech isn't harsh. It's pleasant to the ear, it goes to the heart. He doesn't waste words, and speaks at the right time, about what's true and useful. Then the finer points. He doesn't damage seeds or plants. He doesn't go to shows: dancing, singing, music, those elephant fights. He doesn't play the games. He doesn't trade in false weights and measures. He doesn't pass the day in what the text calls low talk: kings and robbers, food and clothes, gossip at the well. The Pali word for all this is sila: moral conduct, virtue. And here's the twist. The Buddha calls it small. The real teaching is deeper, and the rest of the discourse goes there. But he practices every one of the small things anyway. They aren't the summit. They're the ground the summit stands on.
screen: `WHAT ORDINARY PEOPLE PRAISE` · `NO STICK, NO SWORD, NO TALE-BEARING` · `NO SHOWS, NO GAMES, NO LOW TALK` · `SMALL, BUT THE GROUND OF IT ALL` · then, large: `THE SMALL THINGS.`

segments.voice: Go through the list slowly, gentle speech, no carrying tales, speaking at the right time, not wasting words, taking only what's given, and let the one closest to your actual life light up. Picture the moment it usually comes, see yourself meeting it with a little more care, then rest with the breath.
Sila. Moral conduct, virtue, in its smallest forms: kind speech, no gossip, careful hands. Small, and still practiced.
Your line: the ground the summit stands on. He called it small, and kept every piece. See you tomorrow.

525.title: The net of views
525.hook: sixty-two views caught like fish in a fine net
525.howItsDone: The Brahmajala Sutta is studied in Theravada monasteries as a survey of speculative views; teachers use it to show practitioners how views arise from feeling and craving rather than to promote a rival theory.

segments.voice: Yesterday: sila, the small things, and your line, the ground the summit stands on. Today ends a week, and the first long discourse throws its net.

Is the world eternal? Did it begin by chance? Is the self the same after death? Will it be destroyed? In the Buddha's India, wandering philosophers argued questions like these from town to town. Some are still argued over kitchen tables and on podcasts. The first long discourse, after the small things, turns to the deep things: every theory about self and world the Buddha could name. He counts them. Sixty-two.
screen: `IS THE WORLD ETERNAL?` → `WANDERERS ARGUING EVERYWHERE.` → `SIXTY-TWO VIEWS.`

segments.voice: They fall into two groups. Eighteen are about the past: that self and world are eternal, or partly eternal, or finite, or infinite, or arose by chance. There are even the eel-wrigglers, who slip out of every question without committing to anything. Forty-four are about the future: that the self survives death with perception, or without it, or is destroyed, or that the highest bliss is found right here, in pleasure or in meditation. The Buddha describes each with care, and how people arrive at it: some through deep meditation that shows them a slice of the past, and then generalize from it; some through reasoning alone. Then the turn. Every one of these views depends on contact, the senses meeting the world. From contact, feeling. From feeling, craving. And from craving, clinging to a view. The Pali word is ditthi: view, opinion, literally something seen. And the image. A skilled fisherman casts a fine-meshed net over a small pond. Whatever fish of any size are in it, they're all inside the net; when they rise, they rise inside it. So with these sixty-two views: whoever theorizes about the past or the future is caught, however they thrash. The one who sees how views arise isn't caught. Not because he holds a sixty-third view, but because he understands the net. Look back at the week: no excuse, yours, the middle way, the long ones, not elated, not angry, the small things. And now the net.
screen: `EIGHTEEN ABOUT THE PAST` · `FORTY-FOUR ABOUT THE FUTURE` · `CONTACT, FEELING, CRAVING, VIEW` · `A FINE NET OVER A SMALL POND` · then, large: `ALL VIEWS, IN THE NET.`

segments.voice: Pick an opinion you hold strongly, about politics, about people, about how the world works, and don't argue for or against it; just watch where it seems to live in the body and what feeling sits under it, pleasant or tense, with wanting or without. See it as something that arose, then rest with the breath.
The net of views. Sixty-two theories of self and world, all arising from contact, feeling and craving, all held in one fine net.
Your line: all views, in the net. Understanding the net isn't one more view inside it. Day five hundred twenty-five.

chat.says: So which of those sixty-two views did the Buddha say was the right one?
options: None of them; he showed how every view arises from contact, feeling and craving.
The eighteen about the past; the future ones are only guesswork.
The one that says the self is wholly destroyed when the body dies.
chat.meaning: The Buddha doesn't add a sixty-third view. He shows that every view arises from contact, feeling and craving: all caught in one net.
